newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan threatens to seize islands protest boats.
newsitem.headline: Japan threatens to seize islands protest boats.

text.p: Japan stood firm on Monday on a sovereignty dispute over islands in the East China Sea and threatened to seize protest boats from Taiwan and Hong Kong surrounding the chain.
But it denied a Taiwanese radio report that Japanese coastguards boarded a Hong Kong vessel leading the protest flotilla challenging Tokyo's claims to the archipelago.
A spokesman for the coastguard, the Maritime Safety Agency, said there were no reports of coastguards boarding the vessel named "Protect the Diaoyus" or any other protest boat.

As some 200 Taiwanese and Hong Kong activists aboard fishing boats approached the islands, Japan warned it would seize the vessels if activists tried to land on the isles claimed by Tokyo as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.
"The Japanese government will take appropriate measures to block (the activists) from landing on the islands," top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference.
Asked if the measures could include seizing the ships, Kajiyama replied: "Yes, that's right."
"As we have repeatedly said, the islands are Japan's territory and they are effectively controlled by Japan," Kajiyama said.
"Therefore, landing on the islands would constitute a violation of Japan's law."
The Maritime Safety Agency mobilised about 60 patrol boats, some of them armed, to prevent protesters entering the 12 nautical miles of territorial waters Japan claims around the islands.
"We must not let them into our territorial waters," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters.
The coastguard spokesman said activists aboard several protest boats started fishing on Monday morning in waters about 37 km (23 miles) away from the islands.
"Through loudspeakers, we are warning them not to enter Japan's territorial waters," he said.
The activists plan to carry out what they have dubbed the "Diaoyu Island World Cup Fishing Contest".
The coastguard spokesman said none of the protesters had tried to pierce the Japanese cordon.
"It has been calm so far. We really hope they will finish their activities quietly," he said.
The activists have said they would not rule out a landing on the cluster of uninhabited islands, which lie 200 km (125 miles) northeast of Taiwan.

The dispute over sovereignty has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands in July 1996.
A Hong Kong activist drowned in September when he jumped from a protest boat into stormy waters during an abortive voyage to the islands.

In a move that added fuel to the fire, four Japanese, including one legislator, planted a Japanese flag on one of the islands earlier this month and spent two hours surveying and holding a memorial ceremony.
Japan took over the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. China and Taiwan say they should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
